main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced concepts, theories and principles of theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the development of theatre arts and its major trends
learning_activity_name: Describe the major trends in the development of theatre worldwide (naturalism, realism, symbolism, expressionism and theatre of the absurd)
sla_name: Major trends in the development of world theatre
sla_assessment_criteria: Major trends in the development of theatre worldwide well described.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: World theatre has passed through several major movements, each defined by a different view of how truth and meaning should be shown on stage.
sla_notes_details: Naturalism (Emile Zola, Anton Chekhov) tried to reproduce ordinary life on stage exactly as it appears, with detailed sets and everyday speech. Realism, closely related, focused on believable characters and social problems rather than heroic plots. Symbolism used suggestion, mood, dim lighting and poetic dialogue instead of literal representation to express inner truth. Expressionism (as in the plays of the German stage) distorted setting, movement and speech to project a character's inner emotional state rather than external reality. Theatre of the Absurd (Samuel Beckett, Eugene Ionesco) abandoned logical plot and cause-and-effect dialogue to show the meaninglessness of human existence after the two World Wars.
sla_notes_illustrations: In Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot, two characters wait endlessly for someone who never arrives, using circular, illogical dialogue that is the clearest classroom example of the Theatre of the Absurd.
sla_notes_daily_life: Tanzanian filmmakers and playwrights borrow techniques from these movements, for example using naturalistic dialogue in Bongo Movies and symbolic costume or lighting in stage plays performed at cultural festivals.
sla_exercise: Name any three major trends in the development of world theatre.::Naturalism, realism, symbolism, expressionism and Theatre of the Absurd (any three).||What distinguishes Theatre of the Absurd from naturalism?::Theatre of the Absurd rejects logical plot and normal dialogue to show life's meaninglessness, while naturalism reproduces everyday life exactly as it appears.||Give one playwright associated with the Theatre of the Absurd and one of his plays.::Samuel Beckett; Waiting for Godot.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced concepts, theories and principles of theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the development of theatre arts and its major trends
learning_activity_name: Explain the major trends in the development of theatre in Africa (theatre for social change)
sla_name: Theatre in Africa and theatre for social change
sla_method: ICT-based learning and Africa Case study
sla_assessment_criteria: Trends in the development of theatre in Africa well described.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: African theatre developed its own trends alongside Western movements, most notably theatre used deliberately as a tool for social change.
sla_notes_details: Theatre for social change (also called theatre for development) uses drama to raise awareness, provoke discussion and mobilise communities around issues such as health, gender, corruption and civic rights, often performed in the open air with audience participation rather than in formal theatres. It grew from indigenous African performance traditions of storytelling, ritual and communal dance that already blended entertainment with moral and social instruction, and was later shaped by practitioners such as Ngugi wa Thiong'o in Kenya who used community theatre to challenge oppression. Techniques include forum theatre, where the audience stops the action and suggests alternative solutions, and popular theatre performed by community groups in local languages.
sla_notes_illustrations: A community drama group performing a play about early pregnancy in a village square, then stopping the action so the audience can suggest what the characters should have done differently, is a classic example of forum theatre for social change.
sla_notes_daily_life: Many Tanzanian NGOs use travelling theatre groups to teach communities about HIV/AIDS prevention, malaria control and children's rights, showing how theatre for social change operates in real community life.
sla_exercise: What is meant by theatre for social change?::Theatre used deliberately to raise awareness of and mobilise communities around social issues, rather than purely for entertainment.||Name one technique used in theatre for social change.::Forum theatre, where the audience interrupts and suggests alternative solutions (or popular theatre performed in local languages).||Give one social issue commonly addressed through African theatre for social change.::HIV/AIDS awareness (or gender-based violence, corruption, civic education).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced concepts, theories and principles of theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the history and principles of scriptwriting, acting and directing
learning_activity_name: Explain the emergence and development of scriptwriting for stage, film, radio and television
sla_name: Emergence and development of scriptwriting for stage, film, radio and television
sla_assessment_criteria: The emergence and development of scriptwriting for stage, film, radio and television well explained.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Scriptwriting is the craft of putting a story into the written form required for a particular medium, and it has developed differently for stage, film, radio and television.
sla_notes_details: Stage scriptwriting grew from oral storytelling and classical drama into the modern playscript, which records dialogue and stage directions for a live audience in one continuous space. Film scriptwriting emerged with early cinema in the twentieth century and required a new format built around shots, scenes and visual description because film can cut between locations and times. Radio scriptwriting developed from the 1920s onward and depends entirely on sound: dialogue, sound effects and music must create pictures in the listener's mind since there is no visual element. Television scriptwriting borrowed from both stage and film but adapted to serial storytelling, advertising breaks and a smaller screen, favouring close dialogue and clear scene headings. Across all four media the script remains the blueprint that guides actors, directors and technical crew.
sla_notes_illustrations: A stage script writes 'JUMA: (angrily) You lied to me!' while the same moment in a radio script must add a sound cue such as '(door slams)' because the radio audience cannot see Juma's anger.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local television dramas broadcast in Tanzania and community radio programmes both begin as scripts written specifically for their medium, showing learners how the same story idea changes shape depending on where it will be performed.
sla_exercise: Name the four media for which scriptwriting has developed.::Stage, film, radio and television.||Why must a radio script rely heavily on sound effects and dialogue?::Because radio has no pictures, so sound must create the scene entirely in the listener's imagination.||State one way a film script differs from a stage script.::A film script is organised by shots and scenes that can move between locations and times, while a stage script keeps continuous action in one space.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced concepts, theories and principles of theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the history and principles of scriptwriting, acting and directing
learning_activity_name: Describe principles of scriptwriting for stage, film, radio and television
sla_name: Principles of scriptwriting for stage, film, radio and television
sla_method: ICT-based learning and Jigsaw Learning approach
sla_assessment_criteria: Principles of scriptwriting for stage, film, radio and television clearly described.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Good scriptwriting for any medium follows shared principles that make a story clear, dramatic and playable by actors.
sla_notes_details: Key principles include a clear dramatic structure (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution), believable and consistent characters with clear motivation, economical dialogue that reveals character and moves the plot forward rather than explaining everything directly, and appropriate formatting for the target medium (stage directions in brackets for plays, shot descriptions for film, sound cues for radio, scene headings for television). Conflict is central: every scene should contain a goal, an obstacle and consequences that push the story forward. Scripts are also written with a specific audience and performance context in mind, considering length, number of actors and available resources.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student scriptwriting exercise might take a simple conflict, a shopkeeper refusing to give change, and rewrite it first as a stage scene with dialogue and stage directions, then as a radio scene relying only on voices and sound effects.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding these principles helps students write scripts for school drama clubs, church plays and community radio programmes that are clear and enjoyable to perform.
sla_exercise: State two principles that guide good scriptwriting.::Clear dramatic structure with conflict, and economical dialogue that reveals character (any two valid principles).||Why is conflict considered central to a scene in a script?::Because conflict, with a goal and an obstacle, creates dramatic tension that drives the story forward.||Name one formatting feature specific to a stage script.::Stage directions written in brackets to guide actors' movement and emotion.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced concepts, theories and principles of theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the history and principles of scriptwriting, acting and directing
learning_activity_name: Describe various software used for scriptwriting (Celtx, Movie Magic screenwriter)
sla_name: Software used for scriptwriting
sla_assessment_criteria: Various software used for scriptwriting well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Software used for scriptwriting Celtx|Movie Magic screenwriter
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Modern scriptwriters increasingly use specialised computer software instead of plain word processors to format and organise their scripts.
sla_notes_details: Celtx is a widely used scriptwriting application that automatically formats stage, film, radio and television scripts, and also allows storyboarding, scheduling and collaboration among a production team. Movie Magic Screenwriter is another professional tool used mainly in the film and television industry that automatically applies industry-standard formatting rules for scene headings, action lines and dialogue, and tracks elements such as characters, props and locations across a script. Both types of software save writers time on formatting so they can focus on story and dialogue, and they make it easier to revise, share and print scripts in a standard format that actors and directors recognise.
sla_notes_illustrations: A scriptwriter typing dialogue into Celtx only needs to select 'Character' and 'Dialogue' elements from a menu and the software automatically applies the correct indentation and capitalisation used in professional scripts.
sla_notes_daily_life: Where computers and internet access are available, students can use free trial versions of such software, or basic word-processor templates that imitate the same layout, to prepare scripts for school drama productions.
sla_exercise: Name two software applications used for scriptwriting.::Celtx and Movie Magic Screenwriter.||Give one advantage of using scriptwriting software over an ordinary word processor.::It automatically applies correct industry formatting for scenes, characters and dialogue, saving the writer time.||What additional production tasks, besides writing, can Celtx help with?::Storyboarding, scheduling and collaboration among a production team.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced concepts, theories and principles of theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the methods of identifying an ideal performing space
learning_activity_name: Describe the methods and techniques of identifying an ideal performing space
sla_name: Methods and techniques of identifying an ideal performing space
sla_assessment_criteria: The methods and techniques of identifying an ideal performing space well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Videos of identifying an ideal performing space
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Choosing where a theatrical performance will take place is a deliberate process that considers the needs of the audience, the actors and the story.
sla_notes_details: Methods of identifying an ideal performing space include assessing sightlines (whether every seat allows a clear view of the acting area), acoustics (how well sound and voices carry without distortion or echo), audience capacity and seating arrangement, safety of entrances, exits and the acting surface, and access to power for lighting and sound equipment. Techniques include physically visiting and testing candidate spaces, walking and speaking from different points on the proposed stage while a colleague listens from various seats, and considering the type of performance: a proscenium stage suits realistic drama with scenery, while an open or arena space suits community theatre for social change performed among the audience.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group planning a school performance might test a hall by having one student speak normally from the front while others sit at the back to confirm every word can be heard clearly before deciding the hall is suitable.
sla_notes_daily_life: The same considerations apply when choosing a venue for a wedding ceremony, a church drama or a community meeting, since sightlines, sound and safety matter in any gathering where people must see and hear a performer.
sla_exercise: State two factors to consider when identifying an ideal performing space.::Sightlines for the audience and the acoustics of the space (any two valid factors).||Why is it important to test acoustics before choosing a performing space?::Poor acoustics can make dialogue inaudible or distorted, ruining the audience's understanding of the performance.||Name one technique used to test whether a space is suitable for performance.::Having someone speak from the stage while listeners check audibility from different seats.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced concepts, theories and principles of theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the methods of identifying an ideal performing space
learning_activity_name: Design an area for staging a theatrical performance
sla_name: Designing an area for staging a theatrical performance
sla_assessment_criteria: An area for staging a theatrical performance well designed.
sla_teaching_aids: Videos of designing various areas for staging a theatrical performance
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Once a space has been chosen, it must be designed and arranged specifically for the performance that will take place in it.
sla_notes_details: Designing a staging area involves deciding the type of stage configuration (proscenium, thrust, arena or open stage), marking the acting area, planning entrances and exits (wings, aisles), placing scenery and set pieces so they do not block sightlines, positioning lighting instruments and speakers, and arranging seating to give the whole audience a comfortable and clear view. Designers also consider the flow of movement for actors changing costume backstage and for technical crew operating lights and sound during the show. A ground plan, a scale drawing showing the position of furniture, set pieces and acting areas, is usually prepared before rehearsals begin.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student designing a school hall for a play might draw a simple ground plan showing a raised platform at the front as the stage, chairs in rows facing it, and a curtained corner backstage for costume changes.
sla_notes_daily_life: The same planning skills are used when arranging a room for a wedding reception, a church service or a community meeting so that everyone can see and participate comfortably.
sla_exercise: What is a ground plan in theatrical staging?::A scale drawing showing the position of the acting area, furniture, set pieces and audience seating for a performance.||Name one stage configuration a designer might choose.::Proscenium stage (or thrust, arena or open stage).||Why must entrances and exits be carefully planned when designing a staging area?::To allow actors and crew to move smoothly without being seen by the audience and without causing safety hazards.

main_competence_name: Perform theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Compose theatrical works for stage, film, radio and television
learning_activity_name: Write script for stage, film, radio and television
sla_name: Writing a script for stage, film, radio and television
sla_assessment_criteria: Stage, film, radio and television scripts well written.
sla_teaching_aids: Drama videos|Microphone|Public Address system (PA)|Stage lights|Visual elements
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This is the practical application of scriptwriting principles: producing a complete, performable script for a chosen medium.
sla_notes_details: Writing a script begins with an idea and a clear theme, followed by outlining the plot into a beginning, middle and end, developing characters with distinct voices and goals, and drafting dialogue that is natural to speak aloud. The script is then formatted correctly for its medium (stage directions for a play, shot list and scene headings for film, sound cues for radio, and scene headings with camera notes for television), and it is revised through table reads, where the script is read aloud, and feedback from peers, to check that dialogue sounds natural, the story is clear, and the length suits the intended running time.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group of students writing a short radio drama about honesty might draft dialogue, insert a sound cue of a market crowd to set the scene, read the script aloud together, and revise lines that sound unnatural before recording it.
sla_notes_daily_life: The same process, idea, outline, draft, table read and revision, is used by community groups writing scripts for church dramas, school debates and local radio programmes.
sla_exercise: List, in order, three stages in writing a script.::Developing the idea and theme; outlining the plot and characters; drafting and formatting the dialogue (then revising through a table read).||Why is a table read useful when writing a script?::It lets the writer hear whether the dialogue sounds natural and whether the story flows before the script is performed.||Give one formatting feature you would add to a radio script that a stage script does not need.::A sound cue or sound effect description, since radio depends entirely on sound.

main_competence_name: Perform theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Perform and direct theatrical works for stage, film, radio and television
learning_activity_name: Perform for stage and film
sla_name: Performing for stage and film
sla_assessment_criteria: Stage and film well performed.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Performing live on stage and performing for a film camera both require acting skill, but the two media demand different techniques from the performer.
sla_notes_details: Stage performance requires projecting voice and gesture so that even the audience at the back of the hall can hear and see clearly, sustaining a character through a long, unbroken scene, and adjusting instantly to a live audience's reaction. Film performance is usually recorded in short takes that can be repeated and edited together, so actors can use smaller, more natural gestures and quieter voices because the camera and microphone are close, but they must remain consistent in performance (continuity) across takes filmed out of story order. Rehearsal for stage builds toward one continuous live performance, while film rehearsal and blocking are organised around what each camera angle needs to capture.
sla_notes_illustrations: An actor delivering an angry line on stage will raise the voice and use large gestures so the back row can follow, while the same actor filming the identical line in close-up for a camera will lower the voice and use only a tightened jaw and eyes, since the camera captures small detail.
sla_notes_daily_life: Students preparing for a school stage play and those preparing a short film project for a phone camera can apply these same contrasting techniques when directed to 'act naturally' for one medium and 'project' for the other.
sla_exercise: State one way stage acting differs from film acting.::Stage acting requires projecting voice and gesture to reach a live audience, while film acting can use smaller, more natural gestures because the camera is close.||What is meant by 'continuity' in film acting?::Keeping a performance consistent across takes that may be filmed out of story order, so the edited film appears seamless.||Why must a stage actor sustain a character through a long unbroken scene?::Because a stage performance is live and continuous, unlike film which can be stopped, corrected and edited.

main_competence_name: Perform theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Perform and direct theatrical works for stage, film, radio and television
learning_activity_name: Perform for radio drama and television drama
sla_name: Performing for radio drama and television drama
sla_assessment_criteria: Radio drama and television drama well performed.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Radio and television drama both dramatise stories for a broadcast audience, but performers must adapt their acting because one medium is heard and the other is seen and heard.
sla_notes_details: In radio drama, the actor's voice alone must carry all emotion, character and action, so vocal variety, tone, pace and clear diction are essential, and sound effects created live or added afterward support the illusion of setting and movement. In television drama, performers combine facial expression, body language and voice as in film, but must also be aware of framing for a smaller screen and often work within a tight studio or serial production schedule with less rehearsal time than stage plays. Both forms require the performer to imagine and react to a fictional environment convincingly even though, on radio, none of it is visible to the audience.
sla_notes_illustrations: A radio actor performing a scene of someone climbing stairs must say the lines while a sound technician adds footstep effects, and must show breathlessness purely through voice, since listeners cannot see the actor at all.
sla_notes_daily_life: Community and religious radio stations broadcasting drama serials in Tanzania, and local television soap operas, both give students real examples of how the same acting skills are adapted for sound-only and sound-and-picture media.
sla_exercise: Why is vocal variety especially important for a radio drama actor?::Because the voice alone must communicate emotion, character and action since the audience cannot see the performer.||Name one similarity between television drama and film acting.::Both use facial expression and body language together with the voice, unlike radio which relies on voice alone.||Give one technical feature that supports a radio drama performance.::Sound effects (or music) that create the illusion of setting and action for the listener.

main_competence_name: Perform theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Use ICT in theatre arts
learning_activity_name: Use digital technology to produce stage and film programmes
sla_name: Using digital technology to produce stage and film programmes
sla_assessment_criteria: Digital technology in producing stage and film programmes effectively used.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Digital tools now play a central role in creating, recording and sharing theatrical productions for stage and film.
sla_notes_details: Digital technology used to produce stage and film programmes includes cameras and smartphones for recording performances, editing software for cutting and arranging film footage, sound recording and mixing equipment for clear audio, lighting control software or apps for stage lighting cues, and online platforms for sharing finished productions with a wider audience. Using such tools well requires planning a shot list before recording, checking sound levels, and reviewing recorded material to correct mistakes before the final programme is shared or broadcast.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student group filming a short stage adaptation with a smartphone can use a free video-editing app to trim unwanted footage, add title text, and export the finished programme to share with the school community online.
sla_notes_daily_life: Many church and community groups already record their drama performances on phones and share them on social media, which is exactly the kind of digital production skill covered in this competence.
sla_exercise: Name two digital tools used to produce stage and film programmes.::Cameras or smartphones for recording, and editing software for arranging footage (any two valid tools).||Why is it useful to plan a shot list before recording a stage or film programme?::It ensures every important scene and angle is captured in an organised way, saving time during editing.||Give one way a finished stage or film programme can reach a wider audience today.::By sharing it on an online or social media platform.

main_competence_name: Perform theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of ethics and professional conduct in theatre arts
learning_activity_name: Describe the rights and responsibilities of an artist
sla_name: Rights and responsibilities of an artist
sla_assessment_criteria: The rights and responsibilities of an artist.
sla_teaching_aids: Videos of rights|Responsibilities of an artist
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Being a theatre artist involves both rights that protect the artist's work and interests, and responsibilities toward the audience, colleagues and society.
sla_notes_details: The rights of an artist include the right to be credited for their work, the right to fair payment or royalties, intellectual property rights over original scripts and performances (copyright), and the right to safe working conditions. Responsibilities include respecting the intellectual property of others by not plagiarising scripts, honouring contracts and rehearsal schedules, presenting work that is truthful and does not incite hatred or violence, and treating fellow cast and crew members with professionalism and respect. Balancing these rights and responsibilities protects both the individual artist and the wider theatre industry.
sla_notes_illustrations: A playwright whose script is copied and performed by another group without permission or payment has had their copyright, an artist's right, violated, and can seek redress through the relevant arts or copyright body.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding artists' rights and responsibilities helps students who join school drama clubs or community theatre groups to negotiate fairly and behave professionally when they later work as performers or writers.
sla_exercise: State one right of an artist.::The right to be credited for their work (or fair payment, or copyright over their original work).||State one responsibility of an artist.::Respecting the intellectual property of others by not plagiarising scripts (or honouring contracts and rehearsal schedules).||What can an artist do if their copyright is violated?::Seek redress through the relevant arts or copyright regulatory body.

main_competence_name: Perform theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of ethics and professional conduct in theatre arts
learning_activity_name: Identify the regulatory institutions and organisations dealing with the rights of an artist
sla_name: Regulatory institutions and organisations dealing with artists' rights
sla_assessment_criteria: The regulatory institutions and organisations dealing with the rights of an artist well identified.
sla_teaching_aids: Videos of rights|Responsibilities of an artist
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Several institutions and organisations exist specifically to protect and promote the rights of artists, including those working in theatre.
sla_notes_details: These bodies include national copyright offices that register and protect original creative works, arts councils and cultural bodies that set standards and support artists professionally, performing rights and collecting societies that ensure artists are paid when their work is used commercially, and trade or professional associations of actors, writers and directors that represent artists' interests and mediate disputes. Knowing which institution to approach for a particular problem, for example copyright infringement versus unfair contract terms, helps an artist seek appropriate protection quickly.
sla_notes_illustrations: A musician or playwright in Tanzania who wants their song or script formally protected would register it with the relevant national copyright office so that any unauthorised use can be legally challenged.
sla_notes_daily_life: Community drama groups that want to protect an original play they have written can approach these same regulatory institutions, just as musicians protect their songs.
sla_exercise: Name one type of institution that protects artists' rights.::A national copyright office (or an arts council, or a performing rights/collecting society).||What is the main function of a performing rights or collecting society?::To ensure artists are paid when their work is used commercially by others.||Why should an artist know which regulatory institution to approach for a given problem?::So they can seek the correct and quickest form of protection or redress for that specific issue.

main_competence_name: Perform theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of ethics and professional conduct in theatre arts
learning_activity_name: Discuss ethical issues in theatrical productions focusing on mise- en-scene (stage and film)
sla_name: Ethical issues in theatrical productions focusing on mise-en-scene (stage and film)
sla_assessment_criteria: Ethical issues in theatrical productions focusing on mise-en-scene well discussed.
sla_teaching_aids: Videos of ethical issues in theatrical productions
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Mise-en-scene, everything visible within the frame or on stage such as setting, costume, lighting and actor arrangement, can raise ethical questions about how people, cultures and issues are represented.
sla_notes_details: Ethical issues in mise-en-scene include avoiding costumes, sets or actions that stereotype or demean particular ethnic, religious or gender groups, ensuring cultural or historical settings are represented accurately and respectfully rather than for cheap sensation, protecting the dignity and safety of performers when staging violent, intimate or dangerous scenes, and being honest about sponsorship or product placement embedded within a scene's set design. Directors and designers must weigh artistic freedom against the potential harm or offence a particular visual choice might cause to real communities.
sla_notes_illustrations: A production depicting a specific ethnic group only through exaggerated, mocking costumes and props raises an ethical concern about stereotyping through mise-en-scene, and a responsible director would revise the design to portray the group with dignity.
sla_notes_daily_life: The same ethical care about how people are shown applies to school drama performances depicting real community issues such as poverty or disability, where costume and setting choices should be respectful.
sla_exercise: What is meant by mise-en-scene in theatre and film?::Everything visible within the stage or camera frame, including setting, costume, lighting and the arrangement of actors.||State one ethical issue that can arise from mise-en-scene choices.::Stereotyping or demeaning a particular ethnic, religious or gender group through costume or set design.||Why must directors protect performers' dignity and safety when staging violent or intimate scenes?::Because performers' wellbeing must not be sacrificed for dramatic effect, and unsafe staging can cause real harm.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the creative use of language in theatre
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the theories and principles related to the use of body language in theatrical works
learning_activity_name: Explain principles of using body language
sla_name: Principles of using body language in theatre
sla_method: Mime and pantomime and Observation checklist
sla_assessment_criteria: Principles of using body language well explained.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Body language, posture, gesture, facial expression and movement, is one of the main tools an actor uses to communicate meaning without words.
sla_notes_details: Principles of using body language in theatre include ensuring gesture and posture match the emotion and intention of a line so the message is consistent, using space and levels (standing, kneeling, lying) deliberately to show status and relationships between characters, exaggerating movement appropriately for the size of the performing space so the audience can read it, and maintaining control and precision so that movement never looks accidental or careless. Mime and pantomime, communicating entirely through the body without speech, are used to train and demonstrate mastery of these principles.
sla_notes_illustrations: An actor showing that a character is nervous might fidget with their hands and avoid eye contact, while an actor showing confidence stands tall with an open chest and steady gaze, illustrating how consistent body language reinforces character.
sla_notes_daily_life: People naturally read body language every day, for instance recognising when a family member is upset from their posture alone, which is the same skill theatre artists deliberately refine and control.
sla_exercise: Define body language as used in theatre.::Communication through posture, gesture, facial expression and movement rather than words.||State one principle of using body language effectively on stage.::Gesture and posture should match the emotion and intention of the line being spoken.||What theatrical technique trains actors to communicate entirely through the body?::Mime and pantomime.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the creative use of language in theatre
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the theories and principles related to the use of body language in theatrical works
learning_activity_name: Describe theories of using body language
sla_name: Theories of using body language: Konstantin Stanislavsky
sla_method: Improvisation and performance and Konstantine Stanislavsky theories Observation checklist
sla_assessment_criteria: Theories of using body language effectively described.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Several acting theorists developed systematic approaches to using the body truthfully on stage, and Konstantin Stanislavsky's system remains one of the most influential.
sla_notes_details: Stanislavsky's system encourages actors to build a believable inner emotional life for a character and let physical behaviour arise naturally from that inner truth, using techniques such as emotional memory (recalling a personal experience to access a genuine feeling), the 'magic if' (asking what one would truly do if placed in the character's situation), and physical actions (breaking a scene into small, truthful physical tasks that reveal the character's objective). Rather than imitating emotion externally, the actor is trained to feel it internally so the resulting body language appears natural and truthful to the audience.
sla_notes_illustrations: An actor preparing to play a grieving character using Stanislavsky's emotional memory technique might recall a personal moment of loss to genuinely access sorrow, rather than simply performing exaggerated crying gestures.
sla_notes_daily_life: Even outside theatre, people naturally behave differently when they truly feel an emotion compared with when they are pretending, which is exactly the natural truthfulness Stanislavsky asked actors to recreate.
sla_exercise: Who developed the acting system most associated with truthful body language on stage?::Konstantin Stanislavsky.||Explain the 'magic if' technique.::Asking what the actor would truly do if placed in the character's exact situation, to generate honest behaviour.||What is emotional memory in Stanislavsky's system?::A technique where the actor recalls a personal experience to genuinely access a similar feeling required by the role.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the creative use of language in theatre
specific_competence_name: Use body language to prepare and present theatrical works
learning_activity_name: Produce a mimetic play
sla_name: Producing a mimetic play
sla_method: Improvision and performance and Self reflection
sla_assessment_criteria: A mimetic play is professionally produced.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A mimetic play is a performance created and communicated primarily through mime, movement and body language rather than spoken dialogue.
sla_notes_details: Producing a mimetic play involves selecting a clear, simple story or theme that can be understood without words, planning a sequence of physical actions and gestures that represent that story, rehearsing precise and exaggerated movement so a live audience without dialogue cues can follow the plot, and often using music or sound effects to support timing and mood instead of speech. Feedback and self-reflection during rehearsal help performers check whether an audience unfamiliar with the story can still understand it purely from movement.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group producing a mimetic play about queuing patiently might use exaggerated gestures, a person pushing into the line, others reacting with disapproving gestures, and a final gesture of the queue-jumper being guided back, all performed without a single spoken word.
sla_notes_daily_life: Traditional storytelling dances and mime performances at community celebrations use the same skills students apply when producing a mimetic play for a school assessment.
sla_exercise: What is a mimetic play?::A performance created mainly through mime, movement and body language rather than spoken dialogue.||Why must movement in a mimetic play be exaggerated and precise?::So that an audience without spoken dialogue cues can still clearly follow the story.||Name one element, besides movement, that can support a mimetic play.::Music or sound effects to support timing and mood.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced concepts, theories and principles of theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the history and principles of scriptwriting, acting and directing
learning_activity_name: Explain the emergence and development of directing for stage, film, radio and television
sla_name: Emergence and development of directing for stage, film, radio and television
sla_assessment_criteria: The emergence and development of directing for stage, film, radio and television clearly explained.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Directing, guiding actors and technical crew to realise a unified artistic vision, developed as a distinct role separate from acting and writing as productions grew more complex.
sla_notes_details: In stage theatre, the director's role emerged strongly in the late nineteenth century as productions demanded a single coordinating vision for acting style, movement and design rather than leaving this to the leading actor. Film directing developed alongside early cinema, where a director had to coordinate cameras, actors and editing to tell a story visually across many separate shots. Radio directing grew from the 1920s to guide voice actors and sound technicians in creating a convincing world using only sound. Television directing borrowed methods from both stage and film but adapted to studio multi-camera setups, tight schedules and serial production. Across all four media, the director interprets the script and unifies the many artistic and technical elements into one coherent performance.
sla_notes_illustrations: A stage director blocking a scene decides exactly where each actor stands and moves so that the story is visually clear to the whole audience, just as a film director decides which camera angle best tells the same moment.
sla_notes_daily_life: Church choir masters and school event organisers who coordinate performers, sound and movement for a program are applying the same basic directing skills used professionally in theatre, film, radio and television.
sla_exercise: Why did directing emerge as a separate role from acting?::Because productions became more complex and needed one person to coordinate acting, movement and design into a unified vision.||State one difference between directing for radio and directing for film.::Radio directing relies entirely on guiding voice and sound to build a scene, while film directing also coordinates cameras and visual images.||What is the director's main responsibility across stage, film, radio and television?::Interpreting the script and unifying the artistic and technical elements into one coherent performance.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced concepts, theories and principles of theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the history and principles of scriptwriting, acting and directing
learning_activity_name: Describe principles of directing for stage, film, radio and television
sla_name: Principles of directing for stage, film, radio and television
sla_method: Jigsaw Learning approach and Gallery Walk
sla_assessment_criteria: Principles of directing for stage, film, radio and television clearly described.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Directors are guided by established principles and theories that help them shape performances consistently and effectively.
sla_notes_details: Key principles of directing include a clear interpretation of the script's meaning and theme before rehearsals begin, careful casting of performers suited to each role, blocking (planning actors' movement and stage pictures) that keeps the story visually clear, and maintaining a consistent style across the whole production. Influential theorists shaped these principles: Konstantin Stanislavsky emphasised truthful, psychologically motivated acting; Bertolt Brecht developed epic theatre and the 'alienation effect' to keep audiences critically aware rather than emotionally absorbed; Antonin Artaud's 'theatre of cruelty' aimed to assault the senses and provoke raw audience reaction; and Jerzy Grotowski's 'poor theatre' stripped away scenery and technology to focus purely on the actor's body and voice. A director chooses or blends such approaches according to the production's goals.
sla_notes_illustrations: A director following Brecht's alienation effect might have an actor step out of character to address the audience directly, deliberately breaking the illusion so viewers think critically about the play's message rather than simply feeling emotion.
sla_notes_daily_life: Church and school programme organisers who plan where speakers stand, how a choir moves, and what mood a ceremony should create are applying basic directing principles, even without naming Stanislavsky or Brecht.
sla_exercise: Name one theorist associated with the principles of directing and state their key idea.::Konstantin Stanislavsky, who emphasised truthful, psychologically motivated acting (or Brecht's alienation effect, Artaud's theatre of cruelty, Grotowski's poor theatre).||What is blocking in directing?::Planning where and how actors move on stage or in a shot so that the story is visually clear.||Explain Brecht's 'alienation effect' in one sentence.::A technique that reminds the audience they are watching a performance, keeping them critically aware rather than fully emotionally absorbed.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced concepts, theories and principles of theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the principles of managing theatrical events
learning_activity_name: Explain principles and processes for preparing and managing a theatrical event
sla_name: Principles and processes for preparing and managing a theatrical event
sla_assessment_criteria: Principles and processes for preparing and managing a theatrical event well explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Written script|Video of processes preparing|Managing a theatrical event
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Beyond directing a single scene, producing a full theatrical event requires organised planning and management from concept to performance.
sla_notes_details: Preparing a theatrical event follows a process that includes selecting or writing the script, budgeting for costumes, props, venue and publicity, casting and rehearsal scheduling, coordinating designers for set, lighting, sound and costume, arranging the performance venue and technical requirements, and planning marketing and ticketing or invitations. Principles that guide this process include clear division of responsibility among a producer, director and stage manager, realistic timelines that allow enough rehearsal, and contingency planning for problems such as illness of a performer or equipment failure. Good management ensures artistic quality is matched by a well-run, safe and financially sound event.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student group preparing a school drama festival entry might create a written rehearsal schedule, appoint one student as stage manager to track props, and set a budget for simple costumes well before the performance date.
sla_notes_daily_life: The same planning skills, budgeting, scheduling, dividing responsibilities, are used when organising a wedding, a church event or a community fundraiser.
sla_exercise: Name two tasks involved in preparing a theatrical event.::Budgeting for costumes and venue, and scheduling rehearsals (any two valid tasks).||Why is contingency planning important when managing a theatrical event?::Because unexpected problems such as a performer's illness or equipment failure can occur, and a plan is needed to keep the event running.||Name one role, besides director, involved in managing a theatrical event.::Producer (or stage manager).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced concepts, theories and principles of theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the principles of managing theatrical events
learning_activity_name: Manage a theatrical event
sla_name: Managing a theatrical event
sla_assessment_criteria: Theatrical event well managed.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Managing a theatrical event is the practical, day-to-day coordination that turns a plan into a successfully delivered performance.
sla_notes_details: Managing a theatrical event involves supervising rehearsals to keep them on schedule, coordinating technical rehearsals where lighting, sound and set changes are practised with the actors, managing the front-of-house on performance day (ushering, ticketing, seating), briefing the cast and crew on the running order, and solving problems quickly as they arise during the live event. After the performance, management also includes striking (dismantling) the set safely and evaluating the event to learn lessons for future productions.
sla_notes_illustrations: On the night of a school play, a stage manager calling cues for lighting and entrances backstage while a front-of-house team seats the audience are both examples of managing a theatrical event in real time.
sla_notes_daily_life: The same coordination skills apply to managing any community event, such as a wedding reception or a sports day, where schedules, seating and unexpected problems must all be handled smoothly.
sla_exercise: What is a technical rehearsal?::A rehearsal where lighting, sound and set changes are practised together with the actors before the performance.||Give one front-of-house task on the day of a theatrical event.::Ushering the audience to their seats (or ticketing).||What should happen to the set after a theatrical event has finished?::It should be struck (safely dismantled), and the event evaluated to learn lessons for the future.

main_competence_name: Perform theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Perform and direct theatrical works for stage, film, radio and television
learning_activity_name: Direct for stage and film
sla_name: Directing for stage and film
sla_assessment_criteria: Stage and film well directed.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Directing for stage and directing for film share the goal of realising a script but require different practical techniques because of how each medium is experienced by the audience.
sla_notes_details: A stage director rehearses toward one continuous live performance, blocking actors so the story reads clearly from every seat in the house, and must trust the actors to recreate the performance consistently night after night without the director's further intervention once the show opens. A film director instead works shot by shot, often out of story order, giving actors precise instructions for each take, working closely with the camera operator and editor to decide how shots will later be assembled, and can correct a performance immediately by filming another take. Both directors must communicate a clear artistic vision, but stage directing emphasises sustained live performance while film directing emphasises control over the final edited image.
sla_notes_illustrations: A stage director watching final dress rehearsal from the back row checks that a whispered line can still be heard, while a film director watching the same whispered line on a monitor checks only that the microphone captured it clearly, since the recorded sound can be adjusted later.
sla_notes_daily_life: School drama competitions (live, one continuous performance) and short films made on a phone (recorded in separate takes and later joined together) give students a direct comparison between directing for stage and directing for film.
sla_exercise: State one difference between directing for stage and directing for film.::Stage directing prepares actors for one continuous live performance, while film directing works shot by shot and can correct mistakes with another take.||Why must a stage director be especially concerned with what can be seen and heard from every seat?::Because the performance is live and continuous, so a mistake or an inaudible line cannot be corrected once the show has started.||Who does a film director work closely with to decide how shots will be assembled?::The camera operator and the editor.

main_competence_name: Perform theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Perform and direct theatrical works for stage, film, radio and television
learning_activity_name: Direct for radio and television
sla_name: Directing for radio and television
sla_assessment_criteria: Radio and television well directed.
sla_teaching_aids: Drama videos|Microphone|Public Address system|Stage lights|Visual elements
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Directing for radio and directing for television also share underlying directing skills but differ because radio depends only on sound while television combines sound and picture.
sla_notes_details: A radio director focuses entirely on guiding voice performances, pacing, and the timing of sound effects and music to build a scene that listeners can picture in their minds, often directing from a studio control room using cues and timing sheets. A television director works with multiple cameras simultaneously in a studio or on location, switching between camera shots live or in post-production, directing actors' movement within a smaller frame, and coordinating a larger technical crew including camera operators, a floor manager and sound engineers, often under a tight broadcast schedule. Both directors must keep performances consistent with the medium's technical limitations while telling the story clearly.
sla_notes_illustrations: A radio director might ask an actor to repeat a line with more urgency in the voice alone, while a television director in the same scenario might additionally reposition the actor and camera to show urgency through facial expression and movement.
sla_notes_daily_life: Community radio drama broadcasts and local television programmes in Tanzania both need a director applying these medium-specific skills to produce clear, engaging content for their audiences.
sla_exercise: What must a radio director focus on that a television director does not rely on as heavily?::Guiding voice performance and sound effects, since radio has no visual element.||Name one crew member a television director typically coordinates who is not usually needed in radio.::A camera operator (or floor manager).||Why does a television director need to consider framing within a smaller screen?::Because the audience's understanding of the scene depends on what is visible within that limited frame.

main_competence_name: Perform theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Use ICT in theatre arts
learning_activity_name: Use digital technology to produce radio and television programmes
sla_name: Using digital technology to produce radio and television programmes
sla_assessment_criteria: Digital technology to produce radio and television programmes well used.
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Digital tools have transformed how radio and television programmes are recorded, edited and distributed, making production more accessible and efficient.
sla_notes_details: For radio, digital technology includes digital audio recorders and editing software that allow clean recording, mixing of dialogue with music and sound effects, and easy correction of mistakes without needing to rerecord an entire scene. For television, digital technology includes digital video cameras, non-linear editing software that arranges and trims footage on a computer, graphics and titling tools, and online platforms that allow finished programmes to be streamed or shared instantly to a wide audience instead of only broadcast at a fixed time. Learning to use such tools includes planning what will be recorded, organising files clearly, and reviewing and refining a programme before it is shared or broadcast.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group producing a short radio drama can record dialogue on a phone's voice recorder, then use free audio-editing software to add a sound effect of rain and adjust volume levels before the final file is shared as a finished radio programme.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local television stations and community radio stations in Tanzania already rely on this same digital production pipeline, recording, editing and distributing programmes, that students learn to apply at school level.
sla_exercise: Name one digital tool used to produce a radio programme.::A digital audio recorder (or audio-editing software).||Give one advantage of non-linear editing software for television production.::It allows footage to be arranged, trimmed and corrected on a computer without needing to re-shoot the whole scene.||How has digital technology changed how finished programmes reach an audience?::It allows programmes to be shared or streamed online instantly, not only broadcast at a fixed scheduled time.

main_competence_name: Perform theatre arts
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of ethics and professional conduct in theatre arts
learning_activity_name: Describe ethical issues in theatrical productions by focusing on mise- en-scene (radio and television)
sla_name: Ethical issues in theatrical productions focusing on mise-en-scene (radio and television)
sla_assessment_criteria: Ethical issues in theatre arts productions well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Videos of ethical issues in theatrical productions
sla_references: TET(2023), THEATRE ARTS SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Even though radio has no visible picture, both radio and television productions raise ethical questions about how mise-en-scene, sound design for radio and setting, framing and sound for television, represents people and issues.
sla_notes_details: In radio, ethical issues include using sound effects, accents or voice characterisation that mock or stereotype a particular ethnic or religious group, and misrepresenting sensitive events through exaggerated or misleading sound design. In television, ethical issues include costume, set and camera framing choices that stereotype or demean a group, showing violence, intimate scenes or vulnerable people without adequate care for dignity and safety, and failing to disclose sponsorship or product placement built into a scene's setting. Producers and directors in both media must balance creative choices with honesty, respect for the people represented, and responsibility to the audience, particularly when a broadcast reaches a wide and varied public.
sla_notes_illustrations: A radio drama that gives a particular ethnic group an exaggerated, mocking accent purely for comic effect raises the same ethical concern as a television drama that dresses the same group only in stereotyped costumes, since both use mise-en-scene to demean rather than represent fairly.
sla_notes_daily_life: Community radio and television stations broadcasting to diverse Tanzanian audiences must apply these same ethical standards so that no community feels mocked or misrepresented by a programme.
sla_exercise: Why can ethical issues of mise-en-scene arise in radio even though it has no picture?::Because sound effects, accents and voice characterisation can still stereotype or misrepresent people and events.||State one ethical issue related to mise-en-scene in television productions.::Costume, set or camera choices that stereotype or demean a particular group (or showing violence/intimate scenes without care for dignity and safety).||What must producers disclose regarding a scene's setting on ethical grounds?::Any sponsorship or product placement built into the set design.
